summary: Inherent Laboratories post-trains Qwen3.6-27B with LoRA and a GRPO variant into Faraday, an 'AI Scientist' that replicates redacted figures from ML and AI-for-science papers. It works in a five-tool harness and calls the Codex CLI (GPT-5.4 mini in training, GPT-5.5 at evaluation) as a tool through a wrapper script. Reward comes from per-task rubrics written by Claude Opus 4.7 and scored by a Codex GPT-5.5 judge with turn-level credit weights. On 310 Replica tasks (242 train, 68 held-out test), the judge rates Faraday above Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on 73% of in-distribution and 60% of held-out tasks, with average gains of 6% and 8%.

claims.claim: Faraday surpasses Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks
claims.evidence: Figure 2: eight rollouts per task, ±1 SEM over tasks; 60% of 68 held-out tasks; mean +6%/+8%. Scored only by the authors' Codex GPT-5.5 rubric judge. The GPT-5.5 baseline is also Faraday's coding tool and the judge's model, so the comparison is Codex directed by Faraday vs Codex alone, under one judge.

claims.claim: The rubric judge reliably captures human taste
claims.evidence: Figure 3 / F.1: Kendall τ with humans 0.19 (rubric) vs 0.15 (baseline judge); humans agree with each other at 0.30. On disputed pairs humans side with the rubric judge 63%, p=0.109 (not significant). Tasks were chosen to maximise judge disagreement. The noise-share result (3 rubric samples ≈ 8 baseline samples, 16 GRPO groups) is better supported than the taste claim.

claims.claim: Humans prefer Faraday's rollouts over Claude and Codex
claims.evidence: F.2: 41 rankings from 11 participants, Faraday above both baselines in 71%, p<0.01. Only rollouts where the judge gave Faraday a large advantage were shown; the authors state this does not show average human preference.

claims.claim: The coding-agent tool is important for best performance
claims.evidence: Figure B.2: same base model trained without the Codex tool performed worse at equal steps and collapsed after ~300 steps. Single training run per arm, measured by training reward.

claims.claim: The gain is not reachable by prompting
claims.evidence: Figure 5 left: 24 generations of automated prompt optimisation on the Codex baseline did not meaningfully improve it. Only one optimiser (Claude rewriting prompts) was tried.

claims.claim: A director trained with a weaker coding tool benefits from a stronger one swapped in at evaluation
claims.evidence: Figure A.2: GPT-5.4-mini-trained checkpoint scores higher on the test split with GPT-5.5; four rollouts per task.

patterns.note: A small trained director delegates code writing to a frontier coding CLI and beats that CLI alone on judge score; evidence is ML-paper replication, not software engineering.
Long-horizon GRPO with multi-sample judge reward and turn-level credit stabilises training (Appendix B.1 ablation, single run).
Per-task rubric judge lowers judge noise, but human agreement is τ=0.19 and the disputed-pair test is not significant (p=0.109).
Cheap-train/strong-eval tool swap is shown, but no cost accounting for inner-agent tokens is reported.

methodology.sample: 310 Replica tasks (242 train ML, 68 test AI-for-science) from 100 papers; 8 rollouts per task per agent; 20 counterfactual variants; 8 full-scale tasks with one rollout each
methodology.baselines: Claude Opus 4.8 in Claude Code, GPT-5.5 in Codex, GLM-5.2 in Claude Code, base Qwen3.6-27B in the same harness, prompt-optimised Codex
methodology.models: Qwen3.6-27B (LoRA r=128); Codex GPT-5.4 mini / GPT-5.5 as tool and GPT-5.5 as judge; Claude Opus 4.7 rubric writer; Gemini 2.5 Pro task builder
methodology.variance: ±1 SEM over tasks; 3 judge samples in training; binomial tests in human studies
methodology.ablations: Turn-level credit (B.1), no coding tool (B.2), tool swap (A.2), prompt optimisation
methodology.contamination_controls: Figures redacted from the PDF; paper pre-training contamination acknowledged and not controlled (D.1)
methodology.languages: Python ML research code; no Java

standards.artifacts: No code, weights, or task release found; contact email offered

biases.detail: The authors build the task space, the rubric generator, the judge, and the trained agent.
Headline numbers come from a Codex GPT-5.5 judge whose agreement with humans is τ=0.19, below human-human 0.30; the same model family is the baseline and Faraday's tool.
The human preference study shows only rollouts where the judge favoured Faraday; Table 1 qualitative examples are the largest-margin tasks.
All authors are at Inherent Laboratories, which presents its own model and invites users.
No token or dollar cost for Faraday plus its Codex tool versus the frontier baselines.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Faraday (the authors' own model); Codex, Claude Code, GLM as baselines
coi.detail: A company evaluating its own agent on its own task space with its own judge, without releasing artifacts. The ethics statement discloses that some corpus papers are by the authors.

verdict_reason: Multiple rollouts, ablations, a prompt-optimisation control and two human studies make the work more careful than most system papers. Every headline number still rests on a self-built LLM judge with weak human agreement, the human preference study is selected, nothing is released, and the domain is ML-paper replication.
applicability: A reference team will not RL-train a 27B director. The usable parts are the pattern of a planner directing an unmodified coding CLI through a wrapper with deadlines and resumable sessions, and the finding that a per-task rubric judge with several samples is less noisy than a fixed-prompt judge. Neither is shown on software-engineering tasks.
